title: Mastering the Rhythm: A Comprehensive Guide to Nystagmus
summary: A clinical roadmap for the evaluation and management of ocular oscillations. This poster synthesizes the complexity of congenital waveforms and the localization of acquired neurological patterns for the ophthalmic specialist.

sections.title: Definition & The Neural Integrator
sections.content: Nystagmus is a repetitive, involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes initiated by a slow phase drift. It results from a failure in the systems that maintain steady gaze: the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR), the Optokinetic System, and the Neural Integrator (NI). The NI—comprising the Nucleus Prepositus Hypoglossi and Medial Vestibular Nucleus (NPH-MVN) for horizontal gaze and the Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal (INC) for vertical gaze—is responsible for converting velocity signals into position signals ('leaky integrator' leads to nystagmus).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: New onset oscillopsia (suggests acquired nystagmus)
Vertical nystagmus (Downbeat/Upbeat) - high risk of CNS pathology
Associated papilledema or focal neurological deficits
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) or significant optic atrophy
Nystagmus in a child with 'Spasmus Nutans' like features (Rule out Chiasmal Glioma)

branches: Infantile (INS): Accelerated slow phase, horizontal, dampened by convergence
Fusion Maladaptation (FMAS): Latent nystagmus, seen with monocular occlusion
Acquired: Decelerating or constant velocity slow phase, often vertical/torsional
Vestibular: Jerk nystagmus, follows Alexander's Law

sections.title: Clinical Examination Protocol
content: Step 1: History - Age of onset, oscillopsia, family history, medications.
Step 2: Waveform - Determine if Pendular (equal velocity) or Jerk (slow drift, fast reset).
Step 3: Direction - Note horizontal, vertical, torsional, or mixed components.
Step 4: Fixation & Convergence - Does it dampen with convergence (typical of INS)?
Step 5: Search for Null Point - Find the head position where nystagmus is minimized and VA is best.
Step 6: Monocular vs. Binocular - Check for Latent Nystagmus (FMAS) by covering one eye.
Step 7: Associated Signs - Check for head nodding, torticollis, and full neuro-ophthalmic exam.

sections.title: Infantile Nystagmus Syndrome (INS) Features
content: Onset: Birth to 6 months.
Waveform: Increasing velocity slow phase (pathognomonic).
Direction: Usually horizontal and conjugate; stays horizontal on upgaze.
No Oscillopsia: Patient does not perceive the world moving.
Null Point: Preferred head turn to optimize vision.
Convergence: Paradoxically dampens the nystagmus.
Inverted OKN: Fast phase goes with the drum direction (atypical).

content.explanation: 1. Fine, rapid, shimmering nystagmus (often asymmetric/monocular). 2. Head nodding. 3. Torticollis. IMPORTANT: Must image to rule out Chiasmal Glioma mimicking this triad.

sections.title: Surgical Strategies
content: Kestenbaum-Anderson Procedure: Moving the eyes toward the head turn (moving the null point to primary position).
Augmented Classic Rule: 5-6-7-8 mm (MR-LR-MR-LR) recess/resect adjustments.
Large 4-Muscle Recession: To dampen the nystagmus amplitude by weakening the 'rotors' of the globe.
Tenotomy and Reattachment: Proposed to disrupt the peripheral feedback loop of the EOM enthesis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Essentials
content: 1. High-Resolution MRI: Focus on posterior fossa, craniocervical junction, and chiasm.
2. Video-Nystagmography (VNG): For precise waveform and slow-phase velocity analysis.
3. ERG/VEP: Essential in infants to rule out LCA, Achromatopsia, or Albinism.
4. Genetic Testing: FRMD7 (X-linked) and other INS-related panels.
5. Lab Tests: Vit B12, Magnesium, and toxicology screen (Lithium/Anticonvulsants).

rows: Present (Greater in direction of fast phase)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: The 'Maddox' See-saw: One eye elevates and intorts, while the other eye depresses and extorts (Di-encephalic/Thalamic lesions).
Latent Nystagmus: Occurs only when one eye is covered; the fast phase beats toward the fixating (uncovered) eye.
Brun's Nystagmus: A 'Double-Whammy' sign of a large CPA tumor. Low-frequency large-amplitude (Cerebellar) looking one way, high-frequency small-amplitude (Vestibular) looking the other.
Oscillopsia Check: If a patient has nystagmus but no oscillopsia, it likely started in childhood.

sections.title: Optical Management
content: 1. Optimal Refraction: Contact lenses are superior to glasses as they move with the eye, keeping the optical center aligned.
2. Prism Trial: Use Base-Out prisms to induce convergence (dampens INS).
3. Null Point Shifting: Use prisms (Base toward the head turn) to shift images toward the null point.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Eye Tracking & Gene Therapy
content: Gaze-contingent displays: Using high-speed trackers to stabilize images on the retina for patients with severe oscillopsia.
Gene Therapy: Successful RPE65 and ongoing GUCY2D trials for retinal dystrophies can secondary improve associated nystagmus.
Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS): Investigational for severe, refractory acquired pendular nystagmus in MS.
